news.title: That 'Unpaid Ticket' Text Is a Scam — Delete It, Don't Tap It
news.excerpt: A wave of fake "DMV" text messages is hitting drivers across the country right now — texts claiming your license will be suspended for an unpaid ticket and demanding payment through a link. Florida's own DMV says it will NEVER text you demanding money or threatening suspension. If you tap the link, you hand your card to criminals. Delete the text, don't reply, and report it by forwarding to 7726.

news.title: A Shipping-Center Break-In Just Handed Scammers 81,000 Customer Lists
news.excerpt: A gadget-wallet maker called Trezor just revealed that a break-in at its shipping partner now touches 81,000 customers — names, home addresses, phone numbers, and order details, some from orders placed years ago. Lists like this are gold for scammers pretending to be real stores, so expect very convincing fake emails, calls, and letters. Don't trust a caller just because they know your name and what you bought — hang up and call the company back using the number on its real website.

news.title: Hackers Are Taking Over Home Routers Right Now — Check Yours Today
news.excerpt: Security researchers just caught criminals breaking into a popular brand of internet router and taking complete control — no password needed. If crooks get into your router, they can watch everything you do online and steer you to fake websites that steal your logins. Your best defense takes two minutes: unplug your router, count to ten, plug it back in, then check its settings for a software update — or call your internet company and ask them to update it for you.

news.title: Scans of 153 Million Driver's Licenses Are Being Sold Online
news.excerpt: Criminals are selling pictures of more than 153 million driver's licenses stolen from a company that checks IDs for car rentals and stores — the FBI is investigating. With your license picture, a stranger can open cards or loans in your name. Do this today: pull your free credit report at annualcreditreport.com and freeze your credit for free at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — it stops new accounts cold. Expect a second wave: scam emails and calls offering to "help" you with this breach. Hang up and delete.

news.title: Fake 'Are You Human?' Checks Are Running Hidden Commands on Computers
news.excerpt: Those little boxes websites use to check "Are you human?" — scammers are putting up fakes. They ask you to press the Windows key and R, paste a code, and press Enter "to verify." What really happens is a hidden command runs that can sneak a bad program in or open a doorway into your computer. Microsoft and the FTC are warning about this trick right now. A real human check never asks you to run anything. If you see that, close the tab.

posts.title: Microsoft just sealed 974 security holes in one day — the update is free, here's how to confirm you got it
posts.summary: Open Settings > Windows Update on your PC and click Check for updates — Microsoft released its biggest security update ever on September 9, covering 974 holes in Windows, including ones criminals were already using. It's free, it's built into Windows, and it takes about ten minutes.
posts.truth: Here's a number that surprised even me: 974. That's how many security holes Microsoft patched in a single day this week — their biggest patch release ever. Most people don't realize that when your computer asks to "restart to finish updating," it isn't nagging you for fun; it's locking the doors behind you. The honest answer is you don't need to understand what any of those holes are. You just need to let Windows close them. The folks who get in trouble are the ones who keep clicking "remind me later" for months.

posts.title: Your laptop says it's full but your photos are already safe — OneDrive's "Free up space" clears the clutter without deleting anything
posts.summary: If your laptop keeps saying "storage full," open your OneDrive folder, right-click the biggest folders (usually Pictures), and choose **"Free up space."** The photo stays safe in the cloud at onedrive.com — your laptop keeps a small shortcut instead of the full copy. OneDrive is built into Windows 10 and 11, no download needed.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that "deleting" and "freeing up space" are two different things. I see folks dragging their family photos into the Recycle Bin to free up room — that's how photo collections get lost forever. The honest answer is: your files can live in the cloud and your laptop can just keep a "bookmark" to them. Nothing is gone; it just isn't taking up room on the drive anymore. It's like keeping your photo albums in a safe-deposit box and taping a picture of the box to your fridge.

posts.title: The FTC just refreshed its phishing scam guide — learn the six tricks crooks use in fake emails, and report them free at reportfraud.ftc.gov
posts.summary: The Federal Trade Commission updated its free phishing guide on September 1, 2026. It walks through the six stories scammers tell — fake "suspicious activity" alerts, bogus invoices, phony refunds, and too-good coupons — and shows exactly what to do if you already clicked. Read it free at **consumer.ftc.gov** (search "phishing scams"), and forward any suspicious email to the FTC at **reportfraud.ftc.gov** — it takes under two minutes and helps shut the crooks down.
posts.truth: Every fake email I see at the counter uses one of those six tricks — a problem with your account, an invoice you don't recognize, a refund you didn't ask for. The story changes; the playbook doesn't. Once you can name the trick, the spell breaks. I keep the FTC guide bookmarked on customer machines so a suspicious email takes ten seconds to check instead of a panicked click.

posts.title: That "unpaid SunPass toll" text is fake — delete it and check your real balance at sunpass.com
posts.summary: The real SunPass never demands payment over a text message, and Florida's Attorney General has shut down fake toll sites before. Don't tap the link — delete the message, then check what you actually owe by signing in at **sunpass.com** or calling 1-888-TOLL-FLA (1-888-865-5352). Report the message free at **reportfraud.ftc.gov**.
posts.truth: These texts work because they land on a day you actually drove to Gainesville or Orlando, and six dollars sounds believable. The crooks only need one panicked tap. Here's the honest rule: no toll agency in Florida will ever ask you to settle up by tapping a link in a text — real invoices come by mail and inside your account. Delete first, then check the real balance yourself. More than one customer has told me they paid a fake toll site before something felt off.

posts.title: 153 million driver's licenses were stolen — check your free credit report at annualcreditreport.com
posts.summary: News broke this week that an identity-theft service is selling scanned driver's licenses for more than 153 million Americans and Canadians — and the FBI is investigating the company that collected them. Pull your free credit report at **annualcreditreport.com** (it's free every week, no catch), and freeze your credit for free at **Equifax**, **Experian**, and **TransUnion** so nobody can open a card or loan in your name.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize a stolen driver's license isn't about somebody driving as you — it's about opening credit cards and loans in your name. And here's the part that surprises everyone: freezing your credit doesn't change your life one bit. Your existing cards still work, you still buy what you normally buy — you just unfreeze for a day when you apply for something new, and freeze it again. It's 15 minutes of work at each of the three bureaus, it's free, and it's the closest thing to a lock on your front door that exists.

posts.title: Acer just made a laptop you can open like a car hood — the Vero 16 latches open with no tools
posts.summary: Acer's new Vero 16 laptop has a latch on the bottom that pops open without a screwdriver, so its battery and storage are simple swaps anyone can do — see the full specs and a photo walkthrough at acer.com/us-en/laptops/vero/acer-vero-16.
posts.truth: I see this all the time: someone brings in a perfectly good laptop because one part wore out, and the only reason it's a big job is that the maker glued and screwed everything shut. Acer went the other way with the Vero 16 — the bottom opens with a latch, like the hood of your car, and the parts inside are meant to come out by hand. Most people don't realize how much of a computer's "age" is really just a worn-out part in a machine that was hard to open. I'd love to see more laptops built this way. Your mechanic agrees: easy access means cheaper bills.

posts.title: Hate the giant Windows 11 Start menu? The latest free update lets you shrink it and move the taskbar — here's the setting
posts.summary: Install the latest free update via **Settings > Windows Update > Check for updates**, then open **Settings > Personalization > Start** to shrink the menu and hide sections you never use, and **Settings > Personalization > Taskbar > Taskbar behaviors** to move it where you want it.
posts.truth: Here's something the tech world gets wrong: people aren't afraid of change — they're annoyed by change they didn't ask for. Microsoft moved everybody's cheese with the big Start menu, and folks came in convinced their computer was broken. It wasn't. The honest answer is that the controls to make Windows feel like *yours* have been there all along, and it takes about two minutes. I'd rather teach you the setting than have you live with something that bugs you every single day.

posts.title: Bitwarden remembers your passwords so you can use a different one everywhere — free, download it from bitwarden.com
posts.summary: Reusing the same password everywhere is how one leaked password empties an email account, then a bank account. **Bitwarden** is a free password manager: it remembers every password so you only need one strong master password. Download it free at **bitwarden.com**, install it, and let it save passwords as you sign in. It takes about ten minutes to set up, works on your browser, and there's no paid plan needed for the basics.
posts.truth: The scary email takeover numbers in the news almost always trace back to one reused password. I set up Bitwarden for customers who juggle a dozen accounts, and the relief on their face when they only have to remember one thing is worth the ten minutes. Your master password should be a short sentence nobody could guess — something like four unrelated words.

posts.title: Windows 10 computers no longer get free security updates — check Windows Update for your free Windows 11 offer
posts.summary: On a Windows 10 PC, click **Start > Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update** and choose **Check for updates**. If your PC can run Windows 11, Microsoft's free offer appears right there — no purchase, no new computer, and your files stay put. If you see an offer for "Extended Security Updates" instead, that's Microsoft's safety net for older PCs — and it doesn't last forever.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize what "no more updates" really means: your banks, your email, and your protection programs all lean on that update stream, and an unpatched Windows 10 computer will still turn on and "work fine" right up until it doesn't. The honest answer is that plenty of these machines can make the free jump to Windows 11 today — but nobody gets told unless they look.

posts.title: Firefox's new update shows how many trackers it blocked right in the address bar — free at firefox.com
posts.summary: **Firefox**'s latest version, out September 1, puts a counter right in the address bar that shows how many ad trackers it stopped, and it loads pages faster with new AI help features on top. If you already use Firefox, it updates itself automatically — or download it free at **firefox.com**. Takes 2 minutes.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize your browser does two jobs at once: it shows you the page, and it quietly tells advertisers who you are and where you've been. Firefox blocks that second job by default now, and it shows you the count so you can see it working. The honest answer to "is my computer safe?" is: safer than it was last week — if you let your browser update itself.
